title: The Seven Ecumenical Councils in 8 days
about: One council a day: what was at stake and what the Church confessed.

items.text: In 325 the Emperor Constantine called the bishops of the whole Church to Nicaea. A priest of Alexandria named Arius taught that the Son of God was the first and greatest creature: 'there was when He was not'. St Alexander of Alexandria and his young deacon Athanasius answered that the Son is eternal, true God from true God.
For more on this council, start its own 5-day plan.

After Nicaea some accepted the Son but taught that the Holy Spirit was a creature or a servant of God. In 381 the Emperor Theodosius gathered 150 bishops in Constantinople, with St Gregory the Theologian and St Gregory of Nyssa among them.
For more on this council, start its own 5-day plan.

Nestorius, archbishop of Constantinople, refused to call the Virgin Mary 'Theotokos' (she who gave birth to God). He spoke as if the Son of God and the man Jesus were two. St Cyril of Alexandria answered that the one born of Mary is the eternal Son Himself, made flesh.
For more on this council, start its own 5-day plan.

Eutyches, an abbot in Constantinople, taught that after the union Christ's humanity was swallowed up in His divinity, so that He had only one nature. A council at Ephesus in 449, later called the 'Robber Council', backed him. The Emperor Marcian and Empress Pulcheria called a new council at Chalcedon.
For more on this council, start its own 5-day plan.

A century after Chalcedon, the Emperor Justinian sought to heal the split over it. Some writings that leaned toward Nestorius (the 'Three Chapters': works of Theodore of Mopsuestia, writings of Theodoret against St Cyril, and a letter of Ibas) were still defended by some.
For more on this council, start its own 5-day plan.

In the 7th century a compromise was put forward: Christ has two natures but only one will. St Sophronius of Jerusalem and St Maximus the Confessor resisted; Maximus had his tongue and right hand cut off. In 680–681 the Emperor Constantine IV called a council that vindicated them.
For more on this council, start its own 5-day plan.
From 726 emperors of the iconoclast party ordered icons destroyed, calling them idols. Monks and laypeople suffered for them. In 787 the Empress Irene called a council at Nicaea.
For more on this council, start its own 5-day plan.

Many Orthodox also hold in high honour the council of 879–880 in Constantinople, under St Photius, which restored peace with Rome and kept the Creed without additions, and the councils of 1341–1351 that upheld St Gregory Palamas' teaching on the uncreated light. Some call them the 8th and 9th Ecumenical Councils. Later Western councils counted by Rome are not received by the Orthodox Church.
